title: Create interview scorecards for every role
description: A system that turns a job description into a structured scorecard so every interviewer rates the same things the same way.

agent.title: Agent
agent.content: An AI that works independently to complete a goal — planning steps, picking tools, running them, and deciding what to do next without you prompting it at every step. Unlike a chatbot, an agent takes action.

model.title: Model
model.content: A specific trained version of an AI. Claude has several models (like Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) that differ in capability and speed. Larger models are smarter but slower; smaller ones are faster and cheaper.

skill.title: Skill
skill.content: A plain-text file with instructions for a specific repeatable workflow. Save it once, then trigger it with a slash command like /research-competitive. Same steps and output format every time — like a macro for Claude.

claude.title: Claude
claude.content: The AI made by Anthropic. Available as a chat tool at claude.ai, as a desktop app (Claude Desktop), and as a terminal tool (Claude Code). The different interfaces are suited for different types of work.

prompt.title: Prompt
prompt.content: The instruction or message you give to an AI. The quality of your prompt directly shapes the quality of the output. Writing better prompts is one of the highest-leverage skills in this program.

rubric.title: Rubric
rubric.content: The written definition of what a good output looks like, in 3–5 scoreable dimensions. Evals grade against a rubric; without one, 'is this good?' is a vibe, not a measurement.

chatgpt.title: ChatGPT
chatgpt.content: OpenAI's chat assistant. The most widely known AI tool — works similarly to Claude but with different strengths and weaknesses. Useful to have access to for cross-checking outputs or trying alternate models.

calibration.title: Calibration
calibration.content: Checking your LLM judge against your own judgment before trusting it: score five outputs by hand, have the judge score the same five, compare. If you disagree, fix the rubric or the judge prompt — don't ship an eval you haven't calibrated.

children.text: A landmark meta-analysis of 85 years of selection research found that pairing a general mental ability assessment with a structured interview produces a mean validity of .63 for predicting job performance, among the strongest combinations ever studied, per [Schmidt and Hunter's 1998 Psychological Bulletin study](https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.124.2.262). [SHRM](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/non-standardized-interview-prompts-can-lead-to-bias) warns that the moment interviewers improvise past the standard questions, they reintroduce the inconsistency a scorecard exists to remove.

This system takes a finished job description and turns it into a structured set of interview questions with a scoring [rubric](#tooltip-rubric) attached, one question per competency, so a panel rates the same things the same way.

Run it as a paste-in [prompt](#tooltip-prompt) once per open role, a saved skill your team reuses across every requisition, or a scheduled [agent](#tooltip-agent) that fires when a job description gets finalized.
Open your AI chat and have it interview you into a scope document. Done means a written scope naming your panel size, your competencies, your question format, and where scores get recorded.

children.prompt: I want to build a system with my AI tool that turns a job description into a structured interview scorecard. Ask me questions, one at a time, about how many interviewers typically sit on a panel for a role, what competencies matter most for the roles I hire, whether I want behavioral or technical questions or both, and how I want scores recorded (a shared doc, a spreadsheet, an ATS field). Then write it up as a scope document I can build from.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: the interview surfaces decisions you didn't know you needed to make, and the scope document becomes the brief for every scorecard after it.

items: Whether an approved scorecard template or question bank already exists to build from.
How scores get recorded and compared across a panel today.
Whether legal or compliance needs to approve new interview questions before use.

children.text: Bring the scope document. Pressure-test it first in a fresh session or a different [model](#tooltip-model) and ask it to poke holes. Then gather any access it calls for: your ATS or scorecard tool (Greenhouse, Lever, or a shared spreadsheet), your job-description source, and your interviewer calendar. The paste-in version needs none.
**Create.** Build and test the system on a real job description. The prompt below is one example; your scope document has the full version.

children.prompt:
Goal: Generate a structured interview scorecard for [role name] from the job description below, ready to hand to a panel of [number] interviewers.

Context: Job description: [paste or link]. Interview format: [one round / panel / sequential]. Existing scorecard template if any: [link].

Rules:
- Generate 5 to 8 questions mapped directly to specific must-have qualifications.
- Give each question a 1-5 scoring rubric that defines what a 1, 3, and 5 answer looks like.
- Assign each question to a single competency so scores can be compared across candidates.
- Never generate a question that asks about protected characteristics (age, family status, disability, etc).
- Output one scorecard per interviewer role if the panel splits topics.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: anchoring each score to a specific 1, 3, and 5 answer keeps two interviewers from reading the same response as a 2 and a 4.

children.text: **Review.** Check the output against your scope. Every question tied to one competency, score anchors specific, no protected-characteristic questions?

**Feedback.** Fix the rule that produced the miss rather than patching the scorecard by hand. Tell it exactly what's off ("this question doesn't map to a real must-have") and fold the fix into the rules for next time.

items: Auto-generate a [calibration](#tooltip-calibration) guide showing example answers at each score level.
Build a debrief template that pulls straight from the scorecard's competencies.
Pair every scorecard with a bias-audit pass so scoring patterns get checked across a full hiring cycle.

children.text: **Measure** with a rubric instead of a feel check. Have your AI chat draft the rubric and a run log in one pass.

children.prompt: From my scope document, write a rubric for judging each scorecard, with 4 to 6 pass/fail checks. Then set up a simple run log I can keep in a doc or spreadsheet, with columns for role, date generated, whether interviewers scored before group discussion, and what I changed. Give me both in a format I can paste into my notes.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: pass/fail checks remove the judgment call, and logging whether scores happened before discussion catches the exact failure mode a scorecard is meant to prevent.

children.text: **Log** every run against the rubric. Note the date, which checks passed or failed, and what changed. After a handful of hiring cycles it shows which competencies predict good hires and which questions interviewers quietly ignore. A single miss is noise, and a repeated miss is an instruction you haven't written yet.

**Make skills** from what the log shows. Once the rubric passes a few roles straight, package the prompt and your corrected rules into a reusable AI skill, so every run starts from your defaults. A repeated failure earns its own skill. [Claude](#tooltip-claude)'s built-in skill-creator skill will interview you and write it, and a custom GPT does the same in [ChatGPT](#tooltip-chatgpt).

One durable failure mode. A rubric only reduces bias if interviewers use it instead of scoring on gut feel afterward. Build in a moment where the interviewer commits to a score before the group discusses the candidate.

items: [Schmidt & Hunter, The Validity and Utility of Selection Methods in Personnel Psychology, Psychological Bulletin, 1998](https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.124.2.262) — The structured-interview validity figure.
[SHRM, Non-Standardized Interview Prompts Can Lead to Bias](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/non-standardized-interview-prompts-can-lead-to-bias) — The consistency claim.
